source.title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.

accepted.question_text: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with constant density, kinematic viscosity ν > 0, divergence-free velocity field u(x,t), pressure p(x,t), no external energy input, and the usual whole-space, periodic, or no-slip bounded-domain settings, what are the most general smooth initial velocities u(x,0) that guarantee the solution exists for every positive time and remains smooth?

evidence.quote: What are the most general conditions for smooth incompressible velocities u(x, 0)

accepted.question_text: Given either an arbitrary infinitely differentiable, incompressible, compactly supported initial velocity field in R^3, or an arbitrary three-dimensional divergence-free periodic real analytic initial velocity field, does the corresponding incompressible Navier-Stokes solution remain smooth for all time?

evidence.quote: does the solution remain smooth for all time?

accepted.question_text: Regularized versions of the Navier-Stokes equations can force regularity by adding a bi-Laplacian or another sufficiently high-order elliptic operator, filtering the velocity, adding nonlinear regularizing terms, or projecting the equation onto a finite-dimensional space while preserving the energy balance. Which regularization should be used for macroscopic fluid modeling, and do different choices matter when physical experiments do not indicate a macroscopic cutoff?

evidence.quote: Which modification should one choose? Does it matter?

accepted.question_text: Can the Navier-Stokes regularity problem be reformulated and attacked by classifying time-dependent solution paths according to their qualitative properties, rather than by classifying initial data, and can such a path-based classification capture enough of the nonlinear part of the equation to address regularity?

evidence.quote: classify solutions according to qualitative properties of paths

accepted.question_text: For the incompressible Euler equations obtained from the Navier-Stokes equations by setting the viscosity ν equal to 0, do smooth solutions arising from smooth initial data persist smoothly for all time?

evidence.quote: Do smooth solutions of Euler equations persist for all time?

accepted.question_text: For incompressible Euler or Navier-Stokes flows, can one develop a useful Eulerian theory of mixed Eulerian-Lagrangian quantities, especially nonlinear commutator expressions involving second derivatives of the back-to-labels map A(x,t), where A is the inverse Lagrangian map assigning to a current position x at time t the initial label of the same fluid particle?

evidence.quote: mixed Eulerian-Lagrangian quantities, in Eulerian variables

accepted.question_text: For the two-dimensional spatially periodic Navier-Stokes equations forced by a time-independent force, all solutions converge as time tends to infinity to a compact global attractor A of finite Hausdorff dimension. Are the dynamics on this attractor conjugate to a finite-dimensional smooth dynamical system, with the remaining infinitely many degrees of freedom transient in a controllable way, or equivalently does an inertial manifold or consistent finite-dimensional parametrization capture the global long-time behavior?
accepted.context_brief: Inertial manifolds for forced two-dimensional Navier-Stokes

evidence.quote: This is the question of inertial manifolds, as open now as it was when it was born

accepted.question_text: For a mathematical turbulence theory based on Navier-Stokes solution paths, can one characterize the relevant function-space measures supported on those paths, including their existence, whether they are time-independent or time-dependent, whether they are unique, which symmetries they possess, how they depend on parameters, and how they behave under stability and bifurcation questions?

evidence.quote: are the subject of a mathematical turbulence theory

accepted.question_text: For three-dimensional Navier-Stokes flow past a bounded simply connected obstacle B, in the exterior domain Ω = R^3 minus B with velocity tending to a nonzero constant vector U at spatial infinity, can one prove realistic upper bounds for the bulk energy dissipation rate?

evidence.quote: A specific open problem remains: to provide realistic upper bounds for the dissipation

accepted.question_text: For classical boundary-driven Navier-Stokes turbulence, can one obtain rigorous results for moments and structure functions of the Eulerian-Lagrangian back-to-labels map A(x,t), including averaged tensor products of A(x + y_j, t + s_j) - A(x,t), corresponding structure functions, their norms, and spatial derivatives?

evidence.quote: much remains to be done in the classical, boundary driven Navier-Stokes turbulence problems

trace.notes: Normalized the single input as the zbMATH resolver URL https://zbmath.org/1687010. The local shard outputs/shards/open-problems-shard-0.csv identifies this exact zbMATH record as Peter Constantin's 'Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.'

Direct shell fetching of zbMATH returned a Cloudflare challenge or DNS failure. Exact-title web recovery found a source-authorized PDF on Peter Constantin's Princeton page whose title page matches the resolver title; this PDF was used as the primary source artifact.
Mapped the PDF into the title/abstract, Section 1 PDE, Section 2 Dynamics, Section 3 Statistics, and references. Likely open-problem regions occur on pages 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9.

Extracted the broad Navier-Stokes regularity question, two concrete regularity variants, the model-regularization choice question, the path-classification formulation, the Euler smooth-persistence question, and the Eulerian-Lagrangian mixed-quantity direction from Section 1.
Extracted the inertial-manifold/global-attractor question from Section 2 Dynamics.
Extracted the function-space-measure turbulence questions, obstacle-flow dissipation-bound problem, and back-to-labels turbulence-statistics direction from Section 3 Statistics.
Expanded the broad regularity question by inlining the incompressible Navier-Stokes setting, no external energy input, and smooth all-time conclusion stated in the source.
Kept the compactly supported R^3 and periodic real-analytic variants together because the source presents them as versions of the same specific regularity question.
Expanded the two terse questions 'Which modification should one choose?' and 'Does it matter?' using only the listed regularization mechanisms and macroscopic cutoff context from the same paragraph.
Converted the source's broader formulation of the regularity problem into a self-contained question about path-based qualitative classification.
Expanded the Euler persistence question by stating that Euler is obtained from Navier-Stokes by setting viscosity to zero.
Expanded the mixed Eulerian-Lagrangian research direction with the source's definition of the back-to-labels map and the commutator involving second derivatives of A.

Expanded the inertial-manifold question by including the two-dimensional forced periodic Navier-Stokes setting, the compact finite-dimensional global attractor, and the finite-dimensional conjugacy objective.
Rewrote the list of measure-theoretic turbulence issues as one self-contained question about measures on Navier-Stokes solution paths.
Expanded the obstacle-flow problem by spelling out the exterior domain, bounded simply connected obstacle, and nonzero far-field velocity condition.
Expanded the boundary-driven turbulence direction using the source's back-to-labels moments and structure-function discussion.
